name: Berlin
info: Berlin is a city on the Spree river in north-eastern Germany, founded in the 13th century by German merchants as the twin towns of Berlin and Cölln, and since then a capital of Brandenburg, Prussia, the German Empire and Germany.

facts.founded: German merchants founded the twin settlements of Berlin and Cölln at the end of the 12th century; it is unclear which is older, and 1237, the year of the first recorded mention of Cölln, was later taken as the founding date of the city.
facts.where: On the banks of the Spree river in north-eastern Germany, in low-lying marshy woodland on the Northern European Plain, surrounded by the state of Brandenburg.
facts.known: The twin towns of Berlin and Cölln; the capital of Prussia from 1701 and of the German Empire from 1871; the Enlightenment under Frederick the Great; the Huguenots and the Edict of Potsdam; the Weimar Republic of the 1920s; the Nazi capital; the Berlin Blockade and airlift; the Berlin Wall of 1961 to 1989
facts.today: Berlin is the capital and largest city of Germany and is also one of its states, with about 3.7 million inhabitants.

t: German merchants founded Berlin and Cölln on either side of the Spree, and the two towns merged in 1432; the Hohenzollerns made the city their residence in the 15th century and ruled it until 1918.

Berlin became the capital of the Kingdom of Prussia in 1701 and of the German Empire in 1871, and by the 1920s it was the third-largest city in the world and a major centre of science, art and industry.
After the destruction of the Second World War the city was divided into four sectors and then, from 1961 to 1989, by the Berlin Wall, and it became the capital of a reunified Germany in 1990.
dyk: The name Berlin is of Slavic origin and probably means something like "swamp"; despite the bear on the city's coat of arms, it is not related to the German word for bear.
ev: The year later taken as the founding date of Berlin, from the first recorded mention of Cölln
Berlin and Cölln merge into the single town of Berlin-Cölln
Frederick I makes Berlin the capital of the new Kingdom of Prussia
Berlin becomes the capital of the newly founded German Empire
The Greater Berlin Act incorporates surrounding towns and villages and roughly doubles the population
The Battle of Berlin ends with the city's capitulation and its division into four Allied sectors
East Germany begins to build the Berlin Wall
Germany and Berlin are reunited, and Berlin again becomes the capital of the whole country

sections.origins:
Berlin lies in low-lying marshy woodland on the Northern European Plain, on the Spree, which flows through a glacial valley and empties into the Havel in Spandau. The area has been settled for millennia: a deer mask dated to 9,000 BCE is attributed to the Maglemosian culture, and around 2,000 BCE dense settlement along the Spree and Havel gave rise to the Lusatian culture. From about 500 BCE Germanic tribes settled in villages on the higher ground, and after the Semnones left around 200 CE the Burgundians followed. In the 7th century Slavic tribes, later known as the Hevelli and Sprevane, reached the region, with main settlements at Spandau and Köpenick.

In the 12th century the region came under German rule as part of the Margraviate of Brandenburg, founded by Albert the Bear in 1157. At the end of that century German merchants founded two settlements in what is now the city centre: Berlin, also called Alt-Berlin, on the site of the present Nikolaiviertel, and Cölln, on the island in the Spree now known as Museum Island. It is unclear which settlement is older or when each received German town rights. The year 1237 was later taken as the founding date because Cölln was first mentioned then; Berlin was first mentioned in 1244 and as a town in 1251, and Cölln as a town in 1261. The name Berlin is of Slavic origin and is usually interpreted as "swamp".
sections.growth:
The two towns profited from the staple right on two important trade routes, one known as the Via Imperii and the other running from Bruges to Novgorod. They formed an alliance in 1307 with a common external policy, though their internal administrations stayed separate, and in 1432 they merged formally into the town of Berlin-Cölln. By 1400 they had 8,000 inhabitants. A great fire in 1380 damaged most of the written records of those early years.

When the Hohenzollerns made Berlin their residence in the 15th century the city lost its status as a free Hanseatic city, and its main activity shifted from trade to the production of luxury goods for the court. Under the Great Elector, Frederick William, who ruled from 1640, new suburbs such as Friedrichswerder and Dorotheenstadt were founded, and Berlin reached 20,000 inhabitants and became significant among the cities of Central Europe for the first time. After 1701 the city grew alongside Prussia. Under Frederick William I it took on the character of a garrison town and armoury, and in 1720 he founded the Charité, the city's first major hospital and medical school. The Industrial Revolution then transformed it: Berlin pioneered the use of steam engines after 1815, became the main railway hub of Germany, and made textiles, machinery, railway equipment and, after 1880, electrical machinery. The population rose from 172,000 in 1800 to 826,000 in 1870 and to 1,888,000 in 1900.
sections.rulers:
Albert the Bear's Margraviate of Brandenburg ruled the region from the 12th century. In 1415 Frederick I became elector of Brandenburg, and members of the Hohenzollern family ruled in Berlin until 1918, first as electors, then as kings of Prussia and finally as German emperors. Frederick II began a new royal palace in 1443, and the citizens' protest against it, the "Berlin Indignation" of 1448, failed and cost them many of their political and economic privileges. The palace became the permanent residence of the Brandenburg electors, and the electors and the city became Lutheran in 1539.

In 1701 Elector Frederick III crowned himself Frederick I in Prussia and made Berlin the capital of the new Kingdom of Prussia. Frederick the Great reigned from 1740, and the city was briefly occupied by the Russian army during the Seven Years' War. French troops under Napoleon entered Berlin in 1806 but granted it self-government. Frederick William IV suppressed the revolution of 1848 and limited the vote to about 5 percent of the population, a system that lasted until 1918.

After the victory over France in 1870 and 1871 the German Empire was founded with Wilhelm I as emperor and Bismarck as chancellor, and Berlin became its capital. The Weimar Republic replaced the empire in 1918, and Berlin remained the capital until 1945, under Nazi rule from 1933. East Berlin was declared the capital of East Germany in 1949, while Bonn became the seat of West Germany's government. Berlin again became the capital of a united Germany in 1990.
sections.life:
Immigration shaped the city early. In 1671 fifty Jewish families from Austria were given a home in Berlin, and with the Edict of Potsdam of 1685 the Great Elector invited the French Calvinist Huguenots to Brandenburg. More than 15,000 came, of whom 6,000 settled in Berlin, and by 1687 they made up 20 percent of the population; many were bankers, industrialists and investors. Refugees also arrived from Bohemia, Poland and Salzburg. Frederick William I encouraged Protestants from across Germany, France and Switzerland to settle and introduced universal primary education. Under Frederick the Great Berlin became a centre of the Enlightenment, and Moses Mendelssohn was among the thinkers he patronised. The university, now the Humboldt University, was founded in 1810 with the philosopher Johann Gottlieb Fichte as its first rector, and in 1812 Jews were granted the right to practise all occupations.

By 1900 about 85 percent of Berliners were classified as Protestants, 10 percent as Roman Catholics and 5 percent as Jews. Workers moved into tenement blocks in districts such as Kreuzberg, Prenzlauer Berg, Friedrichshain and Wedding, and the city's labour movement supported radical socialism. The imperial city built a modern sewer system in the late 1870s and began its underground railway, the U-Bahn, in 1896. In the 1920s Berlin was a leading cultural centre: Walter Gropius, Albert Einstein, George Grosz, Bertolt Brecht and others worked there, and its nightlife flourished.
sections.crises:
Berlin suffered repeatedly. The Thirty Years' War of 1618 to 1648 damaged a third of its houses and cost it half its population, and bubonic plague had killed about 6,000 people in 1576. In 1510, 100 Jews were accused of stealing and desecrating hosts; 38 were burned to death and the rest were banished and lost their possessions. The First World War brought food shortages, and the "turnip winter" of 1917 to 1918 was remembered for generations. In the revolution that began on 9 November 1918, the Spartacist uprising of January 1919 failed and the Communist leaders Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht were killed by Freikorps members; the March battles of 1919 cost about 1,200 lives. The Kapp–Lüttwitz Putsch of March 1920 failed within five days, and Walther Rathenau was assassinated in 1922. The Great Depression raised unemployment in Berlin to 630,000 by December 1932.

After Hitler came to power in 1933 the Jewish community, some 160,000 people around that year, was persecuted and destroyed; after Kristallnacht in 1938 thousands were imprisoned, and from early 1943 many were deported to camps such as Auschwitz. Allied bombing from 1943 and the Battle of Berlin in 1945 followed. Hitler killed himself on 30 April 1945, and Berlin capitulated on 2 May. Up to a third of the city had been destroyed, and the Allies had dropped 67,607 tons of bombs on it according to one source and 75,000 tons according to the other.
sections.legacy:
After 1945 Berlin was divided into American, British, French and Soviet sectors. When the Western Allies extended a currency reform to their sectors, the Soviets blocked ground access to West Berlin on 26 June 1948, and the Berlin Airlift supplied the city until the blockade ended on 11 May 1949. On 13 August 1961 East Germany began to build the Berlin Wall around West Berlin. During its existence around 5,000 people escaped into West Berlin, and 136 were officially killed trying to cross. John F. Kennedy gave his "Ich bin ein Berliner" speech on 26 June 1963, and a Four-Power Agreement of 1971 guaranteed access to West Berlin.

The Wall fell on 9 November 1989, after a press conference announced that border restrictions would be lifted, and Germany and Berlin were reunited on 3 October 1990. In 1991 the Bundestag voted narrowly, by 338 to 320, to move the German capital from Bonn to Berlin, and the move was largely completed in 1999. The Palast der Republik was torn down to make way for the Humboldt Forum, a reconstruction of the Berlin Palace, and Potsdamer Platz was rebuilt.

Berlin is today the capital and largest city of Germany, with 3.7 million inhabitants, and is one of the country's states. Its Museum Island is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and it has the largest Turkish community outside Turkey.

summary: Berlin grew from the twin merchant towns of Berlin and Cölln on the Spree, founded in the 13th century. It became the capital of Prussia in 1701 and of the German Empire in 1871, was divided from 1945 to 1990, and is now the capital of reunified Germany.
references: Anthony Read, Berlin Rising: Biography of a City (W.W. Norton, 1994)
Alexander Reissner, Berlin 1675-1945: The Rise and Fall of a Metropolis, a Panoramic View (Oswald Wolff, 1984)
Wolfgang Ribbe, Geschichte Berlins (Bwv – Berliner Wissenschafts-Verlag, 2002)
Frederick Taylor, The Berlin Wall: 13 August 1961 – 9 November 1989 (Bloomsbury Publishing, 2007)
notes: START: both articles take 1237 as the later-adopted founding date (first mention of Cölln); the settlements were founded at the end of the 12th century and it is unclear which is older. I used 1237 with circa true.

RESIDENCE DATE: the main article gives 1417 to 1701 as Berlin's years as capital of Brandenburg and 1486 for the palace becoming the electors' permanent residence; the history article says Berlin became the residence in 1451 and also says the Hohenzollerns elevated it to capital in the 15th century. I wrote only 'in the 15th century' and left all three years out.
PALACE DATE: the history article has the Stadtschloss built 1443 to 1451; the main article says Frederick II began a palace in 1443 and the protest was in 1448 (both agree).

POPULATION: the articles disagree on the early 18th century (main: about 30,000 in 1700 and 113,000 in 1750; history: 55,000 in 1709, 60,000 in 1709/1710, 100,000 in 1755) and on 1600 (12,000 around 1600 against 16,000 in the table); all left out. The 1400 figure of 8,000 and the 1640s 20,000 are given only in the history article. Huguenots: 20% in 1687 (history) against about 30% by 1700 (main); I used 1687 only.
GREATER BERLIN ACT 1920: population given as 3.8 million (history) and around 4 million (main); I wrote 'roughly doubled' in the event and no figure. Area 66 to 883 km2 left out.

BOMB TONNAGE: 67,607 tons (main) against 75,000 tons (history); both given with attribution. Deaths of about 125,000 civilians appear only in the main article and are left out. 'Up to a third destroyed' is the history article's.
JEWISH POPULATION: about 160,000 around 1933; the later figure is 75,000 around 1939 (history) or about 80,000 (main), so I left it out.
MAIN ARTICLE: the Wall's 5,000 escapes and 136 deaths are the history article's figures; the main article gives none. Kennedy's speech date 26 June 1963 is in both.
1710: the history article dates the union of Berlin, Cölln, Friedrichswerder, Dorotheenstadt and Friedrichstadt to 1 January 1710; the main article says 1709. Left out.
Left out: tourism, airports, sports, economy, government of today, rankings, and the climate and boroughs; the Seven Years' War occupation by Russia has no date in the sources.

The history article's 1900 population (1,888,000), 1800 (172,000) and 1870 (826,000) are used as given. The rulers section says Berlin remained the capital under the Weimar Republic and Nazi rule, as the main article lists.
Berlin's Jewish population statement 'persecuted and destroyed' follows the history article's 'Nazi rule destroyed Berlin's Jewish community'.
